A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same estimator, simulations and EVOLVE-1/REGAIN application, and their supplied contents are readable. V2 includes Appendices A–B; v1 ends with references. V1 mentions separate supplementary material that is not included, so newly included appendix content is not automatically treated as newly conducted research.

before.justification: V1 reports original Monte Carlo simulations in Section 3 and treatment-effect and study-success analyses using EVOLVE-1 and REGAIN in Section 4.

after.justification: V2 retains original simulations and clinical analyses in Sections 4–5 and reports additional simulation results in Appendix B.

M1.justification: The influence-function estimator, DR-Learner pseudo-outcomes and penalized selection remain substantively the same after matching relocated equations. However, v1 specifies K-fold cross-fitting for every observation, whereas v2 Algorithm 1 specifies fitting on I1 and evaluating on I2 without a reciprocal pass. Whether this changes the procedure or abbreviates its description is unclear.

E1.justification: V2 adds evaluated simulation scenarios with different covariate effects and different time-varying baseline hazards, extending the existing synthetic RMST task. The EVOLVE-1 and REGAIN populations and clinical endpoint remain unchanged. Censoring-intensity results become available locally, although v1 already mentioned such simulations.

E2.justification: Point-estimation and clinical comparisons retain trial-only AIPW, full-borrowing ACW, PSRWE and TransCox alongside the proposed estimator. Inference comparisons retain AIPW, ACW and the adaptive estimator. The additional simulation scenarios extend the same comparator set; newly cited related methods are not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New Settings Four and Five specify different covariate coefficients and time-dependent hazard functions. The clinical study-success evaluation adds thresholds of -0.05 and -0.15 alongside -0.1, retaining 50 subsamples and control sizes of 100, 150 and 200. Existing simulation metrics and the concurrent-control size grid remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 substantially expands reported robustness evidence through covariate-effect and baseline-hazard heterogeneity tests, available low/high-censoring results, and sensitivity of clinical study success to the effect threshold. V1's borrowing-proportion and relative-efficiency analysis is retained in Figure B.4(right), rather than removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report 500 Monte Carlo experiments, bootstrap size 50 for 95% Wald intervals, and 50 clinical subsamples. However, v2 omits v1 Section 2.3's explicit influence-function plug-in variance estimator and its consistency statement, reducing the documented uncertainty-estimation options. There is no demonstrated increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: Figures B.4(left) and B.5 add comparative simulation results, and Figure 3(C) adds study-success results for two thresholds. Shared main simulation curves and the original -0.1 clinical comparison are retained. Conversely, v1 Table 2's baseline summaries and reported clinical event-time and censoring statistics disappear.

T1.justification: Appendix A adds extensive proof arguments for Theorems 1–4 and Lemma 1, including tangent-space derivations, censoring augmentation, remainder bounds and variance comparisons. These go substantially beyond v1's statements and explanatory formulas. Assumption 1 also explicitly adds data-source positivity; Assumption 4 and several existing influence-function formulas are relocated rather than newly introduced.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains a doubly protected RMST-difference estimator combining covariate-shift adjustment and selective borrowing to address outcome drift, with robustness and efficiency claims. V2 foregrounds asymptotic guarantees already asserted in v1; the added evidence does not establish a different central contribution.

C2.justification: Appendix B newly explains TransCox's behavior through violations of proportional hazards after marginalizing unobserved heterogeneity. V2 also discusses extension to other survival-function estimands, cutoff selection and a concrete clinical sample-saving example. Existing limitations concerning small-sample type-I error and partially comparable external subjects remain.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies adaptive lasso, Cox survival/censoring models and SuperLearner propensity models with logistic-regression and random-forest learners, and supplies an R-code link. These are disclosures, not demonstrated changes to previous experiments. Conversely, it removes clinical control-cohort counts, the seven selected adjustment variables and their selection rationale, substantially changing reproducibility information.

R1.justification: The expanded positioning adds propensity-score balancing and integrative-estimation literature, discusses survival EIF and targeted maximum-likelihood approaches through Lee and Rytgaard references, and connects the method to customer churn and multi-source domain adaptation. This materially broadens the research context beyond merely relocating the existing literature review.

P1.justification: V2 separates Related Work from the introduction, reorganizes the contribution narrative, condenses methodological exposition by moving material into appendices, and substantially shortens the clinical description. It also adds Software and Data and Impact Statement sections and replaces the prose algorithm steps with a formal algorithm presentation.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains two scenarios, Table 2 is removed, and the borrowing/efficiency figure is relocated and combined with new results in Figure B.4. The clinical figure expands to three threshold rows, Figure B.5 is added, and shared plots change sizing and colors. Some presentation defects remain, including Table 1's outdated three-setting caption.

improvement.justification: Additional robustness checks, explicit simulation-model choices, a code link and inspectable derivations improve evaluation of the central method. These gains are partly offset by removing the clinical baseline table, control counts and adjustment-variable documentation. The added proofs also leave Theorem 4's variance-sign inconsistency unresolved: its displayed difference has the opposite order to the nonnegative comparison derived in Appendix A.5. Overall transparency and validation improve, but the net gain is limited.
